concepts.title: The Three Orders: Clergy, Nobility and Peasants
concepts.definition: Medieval European society was divided into three orders: the first order of clergy who prayed, the second of nobility who fought, and the third of peasants who worked the land, each seen as appointed by God with distinct rights and duties.
concepts.key_idea: The clergy and nobility were privileged tax-free orders, while the third order of peasants bore the burden of cultivating land and supporting the other two.

concepts.title: Feudalism: England, France and the Monasteries
concepts.definition: Feudalism organised land as fiefs held from lords in return for military service, with monasteries as centres of prayer and learning, and France and England show how feudal relations, manors and knight service knitted society from king to peasant.
concepts.key_idea: The manor was the economic unit where the lord's demesne and peasant holdings interlocked through labour obligations and dues.

concepts.title: Changes: Towns, Cathedrals and the Crisis of the Fourteenth Century
concepts.definition: From the eleventh century towns grew with trade, cathedrals rose in Gothic style, and the fourteenth century brought plague, war and famine that thinned the population, loosened serfdom and shifted power towards kings and money economy.
concepts.key_idea: The Black Death killed a large share of Europe's people, labour grew scarce and wages rose, so the feudal order of the three orders slowly gave way.
